options: To encrypt traffic between networks
To speed up DNS lookups
Because there aren't enough public IPv4 addresses for every device
To balance load across servers
questions.explain: NAT lets many devices share one public IP address, addressing the shortage of available IPv4 addresses.

questions.q: When a device behind NAT opens an outbound connection, what does the router do?
options: Forwards the request to a bastion host
Converts the request from TCP to UDP
Blocks the connection until approved
Rewrites the source address/port and records the mapping in a translation table
questions.explain: NAT rewrites the source address and port for outbound traffic and tracks the mapping so replies can be routed back correctly.

questions.q: Why does NAT block unsolicited inbound connections by default?
options: All inbound traffic is encrypted and can't be read
Inbound connections always use the wrong protocol
NAT only supports IPv6 traffic
There's no existing entry in the translation table for a connection nobody inside started
questions.explain: Without an internal device having started the conversation, there's no mapping in the table, so the router has nowhere to send the inbound packet and drops it.

options: Creates a permanent, manual rule forwarding one public port to an internal address
Removes the need for a translation table entirely
Encrypts a specific port's traffic
Dynamically creates translation entries for every connection
questions.explain: Port forwarding manually and permanently maps a specific public port to an internal address/port, unlike the automatic, temporary entries NAT creates for outbound connections.

questions.q: In a cloud VPC, what typically handles outbound internet access for instances in a private subnet?
options: A managed NAT gateway
A port-forwarding rule on each instance
A reverse proxy
A bastion host
questions.explain: A NAT gateway performs the translate-and-track behavior for a private subnet's outbound traffic at a managed, larger scale.
